title: Plugin types: ESM, ESP and ESL (light plugins)
content:
Plugin types: ESM, ESP and ESL (light plugins)
Fallout 4 loads three kinds of plugin file. All three use the same record format; what differs is two flags in the file header (the TES4 record) and how the game numbers their records.
- ESM (master): header flag 0x1 set. Fallout4.esm and the DLC .esm files are masters. Masters load before regular plugins.
- ESP (regular plugin): no master flag. Most mods are ESPs.
- ESL (light plugin): header flag 0x200 set. A light plugin can be a file with the .esl extension or a normal .esp/.esm with the light (ESL) flag set. Light plugins do NOT take one of the full load-order slots.
Load-order limit: full plugins (ESM/ESP) use load-order indexes 0x00-0xFD, so at most 254 full plugins can be active. Index 0xFE is reserved for light plugins, which all load under that one index, so ESL-flagging small mods is how players get past the 254 limit.
Rule of thumb for a beginner: make your mod an ESL (or an ESL-flagged ESP) when it adds few enough new records (see "ESL record limits"); keep it a full ESP/ESM when it adds more.
tags: plugins esl esp esm light-plugin load-order limits header-flags
verified_by: Header flags read from the real plugins in Fallout 4\Data (Fallout4.esm and DLC .esm have 0x1; Bethesda Creation Club vchgs002fo4_bountyhunter.esl has 0x200). 254-slot rule matches FactGuard.ts.

title: ESL (light plugin) record limits: 2,048 or 4,095 new records, depending on the header version
content:
ESL (light plugin) record limits: 2,048 or 4,095 new records, depending on the header version
A light plugin's own new records must use object IDs no higher than 0xFFF. How low they may start depends on the plugin's header version (HEDR):
- Header version 1.0 (what current Creation Kit builds save): new records may use object IDs 0x001-0xFFF, so a light plugin can add up to 4,095 new records.
- Header version 0.95 (older plugins): new records start at 0x800, so the range is 0x800-0xFFF: up to 2,048 new records.
Records that only override other plugins' records (edits of vanilla or DLC records) do not count toward this limit; only records the plugin itself adds do.
If a plugin's new records use IDs above 0xFFF, it cannot be ESL-flagged until they are renumbered: in xEdit, right-click the plugin and use "Compact FormIDs for ESL", then set the ESL flag in the file header. Only compact BEFORE you release the mod: renumbering changes the FormIDs that existing saves refer to, so compacting an already-released plugin breaks players' saves.
Common mistake: the often-quoted rule "ESL FormIDs must be 0x800-0xFFF" is only true for the old 0.95 header.
tags: esl light-plugin formid limits compact xedit header-version 4095 2048
verified_by: Measured from real plugins in Fallout 4\Data: Bethesda's light plugin vchgs002fo4_bountyhunter.esl (header 1.0) has 3,883 new records with object IDs 0x001-0xF3D; every header-0.95 plugin's new records start at 0x800; Fallout4.esm (header 1.0) starts at 0x001. The xEdit compaction command and the save-breaking warning come from Mossy's guides.

title: SEQ files: why a Start Game Enabled quest doesn't start on an existing save
content:
SEQ files: why a Start Game Enabled quest doesn't start on an existing save
A SEQ file is a small binary file that lists the quests a plugin adds that have "Start Game Enabled" ticked. The game uses it to start those quests in a save that already exists. If your plugin adds Start Game Enabled quests and has no SEQ file, those quests may never start for anyone who loads an existing save (the classic "my quest doesn't start" bug).
What is inside: only the FormIDs of the plugin's OWN new Start Game Enabled quests, 4 bytes each. Vanilla quests your plugin only edits are not in it.
Where it goes: a folder named SEQ next to the plugin, with the plugin's name: Data\SEQ\MyMod.seq for MyMod.esp. In Mod Organizer 2 that is <your mod folder>\seq\MyMod.seq.
How to make it:
1. xEdit (FO4Edit): load your plugin, right-click it and choose "Create SEQ File".
2. Creation Kit: the CK has a SEQ exporter that writes SEQ\<plugin>.SEQ; it is run with the -GenerateSEQ command-line switch.
Regenerate the SEQ file whenever you add or remove Start Game Enabled quests.
To test a quest right now in your own game without a SEQ file, use the console: StartQuest <QuestEditorID> (see "Quest console commands").
tags: seq quest start-game-enabled existing-save xedit creation-kit
verified_by: Two real mods from the MO2 mods folder (We People Can Live In, Necessity) checked byte by byte: each SEQ file is exactly the FormIDs of that plugin's own new Start Game Enabled quests (QUST DNAM flag 0x0001); Necessity's 8 overridden vanilla Start Game Enabled quests are absent. The seq\<plugin>.seq layout is used by both. FO4xEdit64.exe contains the "Create SEQ File" command; CreationKit.exe contains -GenerateSEQ, a SEQExporter and the output path SEQ\%s.SEQ.

title: Quest console commands for testing (StartQuest, SetStage and others)
content:
Quest console commands for testing (StartQuest, SetStage and others)
Open the console in game with the ~ key. Quest commands take the quest's Editor ID (or FormID):
- StartQuest <quest>: start a quest that is not running.
- StopQuest <quest>: stop it.
- ResetQuest <quest>: reset it to its starting state.
- CompleteQuest <quest>: mark it complete.
- SetStage <quest> <stage>: jump to a stage, for example SetStage MyQuest 10.
- GetStage <quest>: show the current stage.
- ShowQuestStages <quest>: list the quest's stages and which are done.
- SetObjectiveDisplayed <quest> <objective> 1 and CompleteAllObjectives <quest>: objective control.
There is no "SetQuest" command.
These are for testing. Players should not need the console: if a Start Game Enabled quest does not start on existing saves, ship a SEQ file (see "SEQ files").
tags: console quest startquest setstage testing debugging
verified_by: Each command name checked as a string in the real Fallout4.exe: StartQuest, SetStage, StopQuest, CompleteQuest, ResetQuest, GetStage, ShowQuestStages, SetObjectiveDisplayed and CompleteAllObjectives are present; SetQuest is absent.

title: Precombines and previs: what they are and why mods "break" them
content:
Precombines and previs: what they are and why mods "break" them
Precombined meshes (precombines): to save draw calls, the game merges many static objects in a cell (walls, rubble, rocks) into a few combined meshes. Vanilla ships them in Meshes\PreCombined\ (181,611 .nif files in the base game). Instead of drawing hundreds of separate objects, the game draws a few combined ones.
Previs (precomputed visibility): data that tells the game which parts of a cell can be seen from where, so it can skip drawing what is hidden. Vanilla stores it as .uvd files in the Vis\ folder (1,360 in the base game).
Why mods "break previs": if your plugin moves, deletes, adds or edits a static object inside a precombined cell, the game can no longer use that cell's combined meshes and visibility data. It falls back to drawing every object separately, which costs a lot of FPS and can cause flickering or objects popping in and out. Players call this "broken precombines" or "broken previs".
How to avoid or fix it:
- Avoid editing static objects in precombined exterior cells when you can.
- If you must, regenerate precombines and previs for the cells you changed and ship them with your mod. The Creation Kit does this with its "PreCombine Geometry For World" and previs generation options (on the command line: -GeneratePreCombined and -GeneratePreVisData). It writes the new meshes to Data\Meshes\PreCombined\. Pack the generated files into your mod's archive.
- When several mods in a load order break precombines, players use a patch such as PRP (Previsibines Repair Pack), or Mossy's previs workflow in the Plugin & Load Order Hub.
tags: precombine previs uvd vis fps performance creation-kit prp
verified_by: Counted in the extracted vanilla game data: Meshes\PreCombined has 181,611 .nif files; Vis has 1,360 .uvd files. CreationKit.exe contains -GeneratePreCombined, -GeneratePreVisData, "PreCombine Geometry For World", "Update PreCombine/PreVis Timestamp" and the output path Data\Meshes\PreCombined\%s.NIF.

title: BA2 archives: General vs Textures, what goes inside, and naming
content:
BA2 archives: General vs Textures, what goes inside, and naming
A .ba2 file is Fallout 4's archive format: many game files packed into one, which loads faster than thousands of loose files.
Two kinds:
- General (GNRL): meshes (.nif), scripts (.pex), sounds and music, voice files (.fuz), animations (.hkx), materials, interface files, SEQ files and anything else that is not a texture.
- Textures (DX10): only .dds textures, stored in a texture-specific layout. Textures must go in a Textures archive, not a General one.
Naming: an archive loads with the plugin of the same name: MyMod.esp loads "MyMod - Main.ba2" (General) and "MyMod - Textures.ba2" (Textures). Bethesda's own files follow the same pattern (DLCCoast - Main.ba2, DLCCoast - Textures.ba2, DLCCoast - Voices_en.ba2).
Make them with Archive2.exe (in Fallout 4\Tools\Archive2) or Mossy's packaging tools: choose the General format for non-texture files and DX10 for textures.
tags: ba2 archive archive2 general dx10 textures packaging naming
verified_by: All 38 BA2 headers in Fallout 4\Data read: 21 GNRL and 17 DX10; every DX10 archive holds only .dds; GNRL archives hold .nif, .pex, .hkx, .fuz, .btr and more. In the MO2 mods folder 468 of 469 "<name> - Main/Textures.ba2" archives sit next to a plugin of exactly that name.

title: Papyrus script files: where .psc sources and compiled .pex files go
content:
Papyrus script files: where .psc sources and compiled .pex files go
Papyrus scripts exist in two forms:
- Source (.psc): the text you write. Your own sources go in Data\Scripts\Source\User\. Bethesda's vanilla sources are in Data\Scripts\Source\Base\ (installed with the Creation Kit), with DLC sources in Source\DLC01 to DLC06.
- Compiled (.pex): what the game actually runs. Compiled scripts go in Data\Scripts\ (subfolders follow the script's namespace). The base game ships 2,422 of them.
The Creation Kit's compiler (PapyrusCompiler.exe) turns .psc into .pex. A script attached to a record in your plugin does nothing in game unless its .pex file ships with the mod (loose in Scripts\ or inside your General BA2). Source files are optional for players but helpful to other modders.
tags: papyrus psc pex compile scripts source user base
verified_by: Folders read in the real install: Fallout 4\Data\Scripts\Source has Base (2,424 .psc), CreationClub, DLC01-DLC06 and User; the extracted vanilla Scripts folder holds 2,422 .pex.

title: Load order rules: masters, patches and the Bashed Patch
content:
Load order rules: masters, patches and the Bashed Patch
- A plugin must load after every master it depends on (its masters are listed in its file header). Missing or out-of-order masters crash the game at startup.
- When two plugins edit the same record, the one loaded LAST wins for that whole record.
- A compatibility patch for mods A and B must load after both; loaded earlier, its changes are immediately overridden and it does nothing.
- Leveled lists (LVLI, LVLN, LVSP) from several mods only combine if you build a merged patch, for example Wrye Bash's Bashed Patch. The Bashed Patch goes last and must be rebuilt whenever you add, remove, update or reorder mods; an outdated one can merge removed or old records.
- Navmesh edits cannot be merged: when two mods edit the same navmesh, only one version can win, and conflicts can crash the game. Use a compatibility patch that carries the winning navmesh.
- LOOT can sort most load orders automatically; read its warnings.
tags: load-order masters patches bashed-patch wrye-bash loot leveled-lists navmesh
verified_by: Rules from Mossy's Plugin & Load Order Hub; these are behaviour rules, not checkable against files. Master dependency follows the record format read from real plugins (MAST entries in the TES4 header).

title: NPC voice files: .fuz, .lip and how they are named
content:
NPC voice files: .fuz, .lip and how they are named
Each spoken dialogue line needs a voice file named after the dialogue response it belongs to: 00 + the INFO record's object ID + _ + the response number, for example 0001A6A0_1.fuz. The response number is the one stored in the INFO record's response data (TRDA). Dialogue (DIAL) and response (INFO) records sit inside the quest's record groups, so the quest and dialogue records must exist before voice files can be named.
- .fuz: the game's voice format, audio with lip-sync data packed in. Some vanilla .fuz files contain no lip data.
- .lip: the lip-sync data on its own (made by the Creation Kit's LipGen, or tools such as Runalip).
Voice files go in Sound\Voice\<PluginName>\<VoiceType>\, usually inside a General BA2 (Bethesda ships them in "<plugin> - Voices_en.ba2").
tags: voice fuz lip dialogue info naming lipgen sound
verified_by: Naming, the TRDA response number, DIAL/INFO inside QUST groups and lip-less .fuz files were measured against vanilla files for Mossy Hub lessons (2026-10-18). Voices_en.ba2 archives seen in Fallout 4\Data.

title: Texture maps and DDS compression formats (_d, _n, _s, _g)
content:
Texture maps and DDS compression formats (_d, _n, _s, _g)
Fallout 4 textures are .dds files. Each surface usually has several maps named with a suffix:
- _d (diffuse / colour): vanilla uses BC1 when the texture has no alpha and BC3 when it has alpha (transparency or cut-outs). BC7 also works and looks better at the same size, but it is not what vanilla uses.
- _n (normal map): BC5.
- _s (specular / gloss): BC5. Vanilla stores specular and gloss in its two channels.
- _g (glow / emissive): BC1 in vanilla.
Other suffixes you will see: _e (environment/cube maps) and _m (environment masks).
Keep the vanilla naming and folder layout (Textures\<category>\...), give every texture mipmaps, and pack textures into a Textures (DX10) BA2, not a General one.
tags: textures dds bc1 bc3 bc5 bc7 diffuse normal specular glow compression
verified_by: DXGI formats read from every texture record in the vanilla Fallout4 - Textures1-3.ba2 archives: _d 2,455 BC1 / 1,422 BC3; _n 2,628 of 2,638 BC5; _s 2,722 of 2,730 BC5; _g 60 of 61 BC1.

title: Loose files vs archives: the INI settings that let loose files load
content:
Loose files vs archives: the INI settings that let loose files load
"Loose files" are mod files sitting directly in Data\ (or in a Mod Organizer 2 mod folder) instead of inside a BA2. For loose files to override what is inside the game's archives, Fallout 4's INI needs, in Fallout4Custom.ini under [Archive]:
  bInvalidateOlderFiles=1
  sResourceDataDirsFinal=
(the second line set to nothing). Mod managers usually set this for you. The archives the game loads at startup are listed by sResourceArchive2List and related settings in Fallout4.ini; mod archives named after their plugin load automatically and do not need adding there (see "BA2 archives").
For releasing a mod, pack files into BA2s: fewer files load faster, and players do not need the INI change.
tags: loose-files ini fallout4custom binvalidateolderfiles sresourcedatadirsfinal archive
verified_by: Setting names checked as strings in the real Fallout4.exe: bInvalidateOlderFiles, sResourceDataDirsFinal, sResourceArchive2List and sResourceIndexFileList are present. The INI values and their effect come from Mossy's guides; they are not machine-checked here.

title: Cleaning a plugin in xEdit: ITM and UDR records
content:
Cleaning a plugin in xEdit: ITM and UDR records
Before releasing a mod, clean it in xEdit (FO4Edit):
- ITM ("Identical To Master"): records your plugin contains that are exactly the same as in the master. They do nothing except override other mods' changes to the same records. xEdit's command: Remove "Identical to Master" records.
- UDR (deleted references): placed objects your plugin deletes. Deleting a reference other mods may use causes crashes; xEdit's command "Undelete and Disable References" turns them into disabled references instead.
- Quick Auto Clean runs both in one step.
Clean your own plugin before release, then check it with xEdit's Check for Errors; you do not need to clean the official master files (Fallout4.esm, DLC .esm) to release a mod.
tags: xedit fo4edit clean itm udr identical-to-master deleted-references quick-auto-clean
verified_by: Command names checked as strings in the real FO4xEdit64.exe: Identical to Master, Remove "Identical to Master" records, Undelete and Disable References, Quick Auto Clean, Compact FormIDs for ESL. The advice on when to clean comes from Mossy's guides.

title: Record types: what is inside a plugin (STAT, KYWD, OMOD, COBJ, LVLI, QUST and more)
content:
Record types: what is inside a plugin (STAT, KYWD, OMOD, COBJ, LVLI, QUST and more)
A plugin is a list of records. Each record has a four-letter type. Fallout4.esm contains 126 types; the ones beginners meet first:
- STAT: static objects (walls, rocks, props); the most common type (19,368 in Fallout4.esm). SCOL: static collections.
- WEAP, ARMO (armour) and ARMA (armour addon: the mesh worn for each race), MISC (junk and misc items), BOOK, ALCH (aid and food), AMMO.
- NPC_ (characters), RACE, FACT (factions), VTYP (voice types).
- QUST (quests; 1,336 in Fallout4.esm). Dialogue topics (DIAL), their responses (INFO) and scenes (SCEN) are stored inside each quest's records, not as separate top-level groups. PACK: AI packages.
- KYWD (keywords; 3,539): tags many systems check, such as weapon types, workbench categories and mod slots.
- OMOD (object modifications; 2,409): weapon and armour mods attached at workbenches. COBJ (constructible objects; 2,161): crafting and workbench recipes.
- LVLI, LVLN (leveled items and leveled NPCs): the lists that decide what spawns, scaled to the player's level.
- GLOB (global variables), GMST (game settings), MESG (messages), TERM (terminals), FLST (form lists), MGEF (magic effects), PERK.
When two plugins change the same record, the last one in the load order wins (see "Load order rules").
tags: records record-types stat kywd omod cobj lvli qust npc weap armo esm plugin-structure
verified_by: Top-level record groups and record counts read directly from the real Fallout4.esm in Fallout 4\Data (126 types; counts quoted are from that file). DIAL, INFO and SCEN confirmed absent as top-level groups (they are nested inside QUST groups).

title: How a quest is built: stages, objectives, aliases, scripts and dialogue
content:
How a quest is built: stages, objectives, aliases, scripts and dialogue
A quest (QUST record) is the container for a story, a radiant task or a background system. Its main parts:
- Stages: numbered steps (10, 20, 30...). The quest moves forward when something sets a stage (SetStage in a script, a dialogue response's script fragment, or the console for testing). Each stage can run a script fragment and can complete the quest.
- Objectives: the lines the player sees in the Pip-Boy ("Find the holotape"). Stages show, complete or fail them. Many quests have stages but no objectives: background and system quests the player never sees.
- Aliases: named slots the quest fills with references (a specific NPC, an item, a marker) or locations when it starts. Most of the quest's logic, dialogue conditions, packages and scripts point at aliases instead of fixed objects, which is what lets one quest work with different actors and places. Reference aliases are by far the most used feature.
- Scripts: a quest script (on the quest itself) plus fragments on stages, aliases and dialogue.
- Dialogue: dialogue topics (DIAL), their responses (INFO) and scenes (SCEN) are stored inside the quest. A response has the spoken text, an optional condition list (who can say it, when) and a response number used to name its voice file.
- Start Game Enabled: the quest starts automatically when a game begins; for existing saves it also needs a SEQ file (see "SEQ files").
tags: quest stages objectives aliases dialogue info scene scripts start-game-enabled creation-kit
verified_by: Counted in the real Fallout4.esm: 1,336 QUST records; 949 have stages (INDX), 257 have objectives (QOBJ), 1,192 have reference aliases (ALST), 438 location aliases (ALLS), 920 have scripts (VMAD), 274 are Start Game Enabled. All 35,443 DIAL records sit in quest-children groups (group type 10) under the QUST top group, as do SCEN; of 78,087 INFO records, 67,708 have response text (NAM1) and response data (TRDA) and 32,778 have conditions (CTDA).

title: How an NPC is built: race, class, voice type, templates and leveled NPCs
content:
How an NPC is built: race, class, voice type, templates and leveled NPCs
An NPC (NPC_ record) is the actor template the game spawns. Every NPC has:
- a race (RNAM) and a class (CNAM), plus base stats and flags (essential, unique, level and so on).
Most also have a voice type (VTCK: which voice files it uses; must match the voice type folder its dialogue is recorded under), factions, an outfit (DOFT: the clothing it spawns wearing) and often perks and scripts.
Templates: most vanilla NPCs do not define everything themselves. They point to a template (TPLT), another NPC or a leveled NPC list, and inherit chosen parts from it (traits, stats, inventory, AI and so on), so many variants can share one setup. Leveled NPC lists (LVLN) pick a different actor depending on the player's level; raiders and settlers are built this way.
For a new companion or quest NPC, start by duplicating a similar vanilla NPC in the Creation Kit, give it a unique Editor ID, and check which parts its template controls before editing them, since template-controlled fields ignore your edits.
tags: npc actor race class voice-type template leveled-npc lvln outfit faction creation-kit
verified_by: Counted in the real Fallout4.esm: 3,015 NPC_ records; all have RNAM (race), CNAM (class) and ACBS (base config); 2,764 have VTCK (voice type), 2,289 have TPLT (template), 2,579 factions (SNAM), 2,181 default outfits (DOFT), 1,361 perks (PRKR), 382 scripts (VMAD); 228 LVLN leveled NPC lists. Template inheritance and the duplicate-and-edit workflow are standard Creation Kit behaviour described in Mossy's guides.

title: Workshop and settlement building: how an object gets into the build menu
content:
Workshop and settlement building: how an object gets into the build menu
Something buildable in a settlement is a crafting recipe (COBJ record) that creates the object (a static, furniture, activator, container...) and costs components. Three things put it in the workshop menu:
1. The recipe's workbench keyword (BNAM) is one of the WorkshopWorkbenchType keywords (Settlement, Exterior, Furniture, Decorations, Power, Crafting, InteriorOnly, Wire), which says which workshop mode can build it.
2. The recipe's category keyword (FNAM) is a WorkshopRecipeFilter keyword: the menu tab it appears under.
3. That category is part of the build-menu tree: form lists (FLST) for the top-level tabs, such as WorkshopMenu01Build, WorkshopMenu01Furniture and WorkshopMenu01Decor, each holding sub-tab lists such as WorkshopMenu01Build02Wood and WorkshopMenu01Build02Metal.
Chems and food work the same way at other benches: the recipe names the bench (WorkbenchChemlab, WorkbenchCooking) and a category (RecipeDrug, RecipeHealing, RecipeRoast, RecipeSoup...).
To add your own buildable item: create the object, create a COBJ that creates it with a WorkshopWorkbenchType keyword and a WorkshopRecipeFilter category, and give it components. Adding a brand-new menu tab means adding a keyword and editing the vanilla menu form lists, which conflicts with other settlement mods unless you use a shared framework that injects menus.
tags: workshop settlement build-menu cobj recipe workbench keyword workshoprecipefilter flst chemlab cooking
verified_by: Read from the real Fallout4.esm: 35 FLST records named WorkshopMenu* (WorkshopMenu01Build, WorkshopMenu01Furniture, WorkshopMenu01Decor and sub-lists such as WorkshopMenu01Build02Wood); 177 KYWD WorkshopRecipeFilter*; 8 WorkshopWorkbenchType* keywords; COBJ recipes naming WorkshopWorkbenchType* keywords create statics, furniture, activators and containers (Furniture 143, Exterior 135, Settlement 76, Power 25, Decorations 21, Crafting 9); chem/food recipes use BNAM WorkbenchChemlab/WorkbenchCooking with FNAM RecipeDrug/RecipeHealing/RecipeRoast/RecipePoison/RecipeSoup/RecipeBeverage. The advice about new menu tabs conflicting comes from Mossy's guides.

title: Weapons, weapon mods (OMODs), attach points and mod crafting
content:
Weapons, weapon mods (OMODs), attach points and mod crafting
A weapon (WEAP record) is the base gun or melee weapon. Its visible parts and stats come from object modifications (OMOD records): receivers, barrels, grips, magazines, sights, muzzles and so on.
- Attach points: an OMOD fits into an attach point on the weapon or armour, identified by an ap_ keyword such as ap_gun_receiver, ap_gun_Barrel, ap_gun_Grip or ap_gun_Foregrip (vanilla has 192 ap_ keywords). The weapon lists which attach points it has; each OMOD says which attach point it goes into and which new attach points it adds (a receiver adds the points for its parts).
- Object template: a weapon's default combination of mods (OBTE) decides how it spawns.
- Material swaps: ma_ keywords and material-swap records change a part's look without a new mesh.
Crafting mods: each mod has a recipe (COBJ) that creates the OMOD and costs components. These recipes name no workbench; they show up when the player mods an item at a weapons or armour workbench, for whichever mods fit that item's attach points.
To add a new weapon mod: make the OMOD (attach point, mesh, property changes), give it a COBJ recipe, and make sure it uses an attach point the target weapon has. Add it to the weapon's object template only if it should spawn on the weapon.
tags: weapon weap omod object-modification attach-point ap keyword material-swap cobj crafting workbench
verified_by: Read from the real Fallout4.esm: 252 WEAP records (113 with an object template OBTE, 111 with attach parent slots APPR, 244 with keywords); 2,409 OMOD records; 192 KYWD ap_* keywords (including ap_gun_receiver, ap_gun_Barrel, ap_gun_Grip, ap_gun_Foregrip) and 163 ma_* keywords; all 1,481 COBJ recipes that create an OMOD have no workbench keyword (BNAM). How the workbench lists fitting mods is standard game behaviour described in Mossy's guides.

title: How the world is stored: worldspaces, cells, placed references, persistence and navmesh
content:
How the world is stored: worldspaces, cells, placed references, persistence and navmesh
- Worldspaces (WRLD): large outdoor maps. Fallout4.esm has 5: Commonwealth (the main map), DiamondCity, DiamondCityFX, Goodneighbor and SanctuaryHillsWorld.
- Cells (CELL): the world is divided into cells. Interior cells are self-contained rooms and buildings (1,195 in Fallout4.esm); exterior cells are the grid squares of a worldspace (38,965).
- Placed references: everything placed in a cell is a reference to a base object: REFR for objects (walls, items, markers) and ACHR for actors (placed NPCs). Fallout4.esm places about 1.25 million.
- Persistent vs temporary: most references are temporary, loaded only when their cell is loaded (1.19 million). A small set are persistent (about 62,700), always available to the game even when their cell is not loaded. Make a reference persistent when a quest alias, a script or a package must find it from elsewhere; leave everything else temporary, because every persistent reference costs memory in every save.
- Navmesh (NAVM) and landscape (LAND) belong to each cell (7,894 navmeshes in Fallout4.esm). Navmesh is what NPCs walk on. Two mods that edit the same cell's navmesh conflict, and only one can win (see "Load order rules").
- Editing a cell: moving or deleting objects in a precombined exterior cell breaks its precombines and previs (see "Precombines and previs"). Prefer disabling over deleting vanilla references.
tags: world worldspace cell interior exterior reference refr achr persistent temporary navmesh landscape
verified_by: Counted in the real Fallout4.esm: 5 WRLD (Commonwealth, DiamondCityFX, DiamondCity, Goodneighbor, SanctuaryHillsWorld); 40,165 CELL (1,195 in interior blocks, 38,965 in exterior blocks); persistent-children groups hold 61,874 REFR and 866 ACHR, temporary-children groups hold 1,182,654 REFR, 6,749 ACHR, 7,894 NAVM and 37,020 LAND. When to make references persistent, and preferring disable over delete, are standard Creation Kit practice described in Mossy's guides.

title: Leveled lists (LVLI, LVLN): how loot and spawns are chosen
content:
Leveled lists (LVLI, LVLN): how loot and spawns are chosen
A leveled list picks what to give or spawn from a list of entries, each with a minimum player level and a count. Leveled item lists (LVLI) fill containers, vendors and NPC inventories; leveled NPC lists (LVLN) choose which actor spawns. Fallout4.esm has 2,098 LVLI and 228 LVLN, usually with around 5 entries each (the largest has 131).
Settings on every list (names as xEdit shows them):
- Chance None: the percentage chance the list gives nothing at all.
- Calculate from all levels <= player's level: pick from every entry the player has reached, instead of only the highest-level ones.
- Calculate for each item in count: roll again for each item when the count is more than one.
- Use All: give every entry instead of picking one.
Lists can contain other lists, which is how vanilla builds layered loot tables.
Modding tip: to add your item to vanilla loot, add an entry to the vanilla list. If several mods edit the same list, only the last one in the load order wins, so players need a merged patch (for example the Bashed Patch; see "Load order rules").

title: Holotapes and terminals
content:
Holotapes and terminals
- Holotapes (NOTE records, 167 in Fallout4.esm): most play a recorded voice or sound when the player plays them in the Pip-Boy (160 have a sound attached); a few run a Pip-Boy program or game (7). The record points to the sound it plays.
- Terminals (TERM records, 778): the computer screens. A terminal has a menu of entries (about 3 on average), each of which can show body text, open a sub-menu, or run a script fragment (207 vanilla terminals have scripts), for example to unlock a door or disable a turret.
Both are placed in the world (or given to the player) like any other object.

title: Sound, music and voice file formats
content:
Sound, music and voice file formats
- Voice lines: .fuz files (audio plus lip-sync), named after their dialogue response (see "NPC voice files"). Vanilla has about 158,000.
- Sound effects: .xwm (compressed, most vanilla effects: about 9,400) or .wav (about 2,400).
- Music: .xwm in Music\.
Sounds are not played from a file path directly: a sound descriptor record (SNDR, 5,475 in Fallout4.esm) points at one or more files and sets things like random variation and conditions; objects, effects and scripts refer to the descriptor. To add a sound: put the file under Sound\, make a descriptor for it, and point your object or script at the descriptor. Audio goes in a General BA2 (Bethesda's voice files are in their own "- Voices_en.ba2").

title: F4SE (Fallout 4 Script Extender): install, launch, versions and plugins
content:
F4SE (Fallout 4 Script Extender): install, launch, versions and plugins
F4SE adds extra Papyrus functions and lets native plugins (.dll files) run, without changing the game's files on disk. Many mods require it.
- Install: copy F4SE's core .dll, f4se_loader.exe and its Data folder into the Fallout 4 game folder (the folder with Fallout4.exe). The Data folder adds F4SE's own Papyrus scripts.
- Launch: start the game with f4se_loader.exe, not Fallout4.exe. Mod Organizer 2 and Vortex can launch it for you.
- Versions: F4SE is tied to an exact game version, and its core file is named after it: f4se_1_11_240.dll is for Fallout4.exe 1.11.240. When Steam updates the game, F4SE stops working until a matching F4SE is released, so many players block game updates. Only the current Steam and GOG versions are supported; the Microsoft Store, Game Pass and Epic versions are not.
- Plugins: F4SE plugins are .dll files in Data\F4SE\Plugins. Each one is built for particular game and F4SE versions; after an update, a plugin that has not been updated by its author will not load. That is a plugin problem, not an F4SE problem.
- For modders: a mod that calls F4SE functions in its scripts needs F4SE installed to compile and to run; say so on the mod page.

Install steps, launch through f4se_loader.exe, supported stores and plugin updates are from F4SE's own f4se_readme.txt.
